claim: Life-history theory describes how traits evolve through the optimisation of trade-offs in investment.
source: Life-history theory, central to our understanding of diversity in morphology, behaviour, and senescence, describes how traits evolve through the optimisation of trade-offs in investment.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about life-history theory that is part of established scientific knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: There is only minimal support for trade-offs within species between reproductive effort and survival.
source: Despite considerable study, there is only minimal support for trade-offs within species between the two traits most closely linked to fitness – reproductive effort and survival – questioning the theory's general validity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results presented in the manuscript and references to prior literature.

claim: Experimental enlargement of brood size caused reduced parental survival.
source: Experimental enlargement of brood size caused reduced parental survival.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the meta-analysis of experimental studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effect size of brood size manipulation was small.
source: However, the effect size of brood size manipulation was small and opposite to the effect of phenotypic quality, as we found that individuals that naturally produced larger clutches also survived better.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the meta-analysis results shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Individuals that naturally produced larger clutches also survived better.
source: However, the effect size of brood size manipulation was small and opposite to the effect of phenotypic quality, as we found that individuals that naturally produced larger clutches also survived better.
evidence: This is a finding from the observational studies analyzed in the meta-analysis.

claim: The opposite effects on parental survival in experimental and observational studies provide the first meta-analytic evidence for theory suggesting that quality differences mask trade-offs.
source: The opposite effects on parental survival in experimental and observational studies of reproductive effort provide the first meta-analytic evidence for theory suggesting that quality differences mask trade-offs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis results and references to theoretical work (van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986).

claim: Reproduction presented negligible fitness costs except when reproductive effort was forced beyond the maximum level observed within species.
source: Fitness projections using the overall effect size revealed that reproduction presented negligible costs, except when reproductive effort was forced beyond the maximum level observed within species, to that seen between species.
evidence: This is based on fitness projections using the meta-analytic effect sizes, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is little support for the reproduction-survival trade-off operating within a population.
source: We conclude that there is little support for the most fundamental life-history trade-off, between reproductive effort and survival, operating within a population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the meta-analysis results and fitness projections.

claim: Within species the fitness landscape of the reproduction–survival trade-off is flat until it reaches the boundaries of the between-species fast–slow life-history continuum.
source: We suggest that within species the fitness landscape of the reproduction–survival trade-off is flat until it reaches the boundaries of the between-species fast–slow life-history continuum.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the fitness projections shown in Figure 4.

claim: Resources are finite, forcing trade-offs in life-history investment.
source: The central idea in life-history theory is that resources are finite, forcing trade-offs, meaning that investment in one aspect of life requires the sacrifice of another (Stearns, 1976; van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986; Kirkwood and Rose, 1991; Lemaître and Gaillard, 2017).
evidence: This is a foundational principle of life-history theory supported by multiple citations.

claim: Reproduction is one of the most resource-demanding life stages.
source: As reproduction is one of the most resource-demanding life stages, it is expected that within-species variation in offspring production will be constrained by the cost of producing and raising young.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in life-history theory.

claim: The fitness costs of reproduction are largely incurred as a decrement to parental survival.
source: It is thought that the fitness costs of reproduction are largely incurred as a decrement to parental survival, explaining why a species evolved a certain amount of reproductive effort, whilst also explaining the fast–slow life-history continuum between reproduction and lifespan observed across species (Kirkwood and Rose, 1991).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation from life-history theory supported by citation.

claim: Brood size manipulations of birds in natural conditions have provided arguably the best experimental paradigm to test the survival costs of reproduction.
source: Brood size manipulations of birds in natural conditions have provided arguably the best experimental paradigm in which to test the survival costs of reproduction as they directly alter parental care investment.
evidence: This is based on established methodology in the field.

claim: Experimental increases in brood size result in increased parental effort.
source: Experimental increases in brood size result in increased parental effort, suggesting that parents can typically cope with increased reproductive demands (Pettifor et al., 1988; Lessells, 1986; Monaghan and Nager, 1997; Conrad and Robertson, 1992; Hegner and Wingfield, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: The expected increased costs of reproductive effort are not always detected.
source: However, the expected increased costs of reproductive effort are not always detected and the current estimate of the cost to reproduce across studies suggests only a small and inconsistent effect (Reznick, 1985; Zera and Harshman, 2001; Santos and Nakagawa, 2012; Cohen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior meta-analyses and reviews.

claim: The relationship between clutch size and survival was significantly different and opposite between observational and brood manipulation studies.
source: The relationship between clutch size and survival was significantly different and opposite between observational and brood manipulation studies, irrespective of how clutch size was scaled (p<0.01, Figure 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the meta-analysis with statistical support.

claim: Within natural variation, parents with larger clutches showed increased survival.
source: Within natural variation (observational studies), parents with larger clutches showed increased survival (or parents with smaller clutches showed reduced survival).
evidence: This is a finding from the observational studies in the meta-analysis.

claim: When broods were experimentally manipulated, increasing brood sizes decreased survival.
source: In contrast, when broods were experimentally manipulated, the opposite relationship was found; increasing brood sizes decreased survival.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental studies in the meta-analysis.

claim: The individual overall effect sizes only became significantly different from zero when clutch size was expressed as a proportional increase.
source: Although the difference in overall effect size between experimental and natural variation in clutch size was strongly significant in each comparison made, the individual overall effect sizes only became significantly different from zero when clutch size was expressed as a proportional increase.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the meta-analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Expressing clutch size as a proportional increase corrects for the variation in average clutch size observed across species.
source: Expressing clutch size as a proportional increase corrects for the variation in average clutch size observed across the species included in this analysis, which ranged from 2 to 11.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation for the analytical approach.

claim: The effects of clutch size manipulation and quality were strongest in the species that laid the smallest clutches.
source: Indeed, also when using a between-species comparison, the effects of clutch size manipulation and quality were strongest in the species that laid the smallest clutches, suggesting that costs to survival were only observed when a species was pushed beyond its natural limits (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Males and females did not differ in their survival response to changing clutch size.
source: Males and females did not differ in their survival response to changing clutch size (Appendix 1 - table 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, contrary to Santos and Nakagawa, 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis that contradicts a previous study.

claim: The variance assigned to the random effects in the model was largely accounted for by study.
source: The variance assigned to the random effects in the model was largely accounted for by study (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the meta-analysis model.

claim: Species identity accounted for more variation than the phylogeny.
source: Species identity accounted for more variation than the phylogeny, indicating that species vary in the relationship between survival and reproductive effort, irrespective of their shared evolutionary ancestry.
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic meta-analysis.

claim: The dataset included few closely related species, which reduces the ability to estimate phylogenetic effects.
source: However, our dataset included few closely related species, which reduces our ability to estimate phylogenetic effects (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the dataset.

claim: The average effect size per egg from the meta-analysis was –0.05.
source: To this end, we projected the fitness consequences of increased reproductive effort, starting with the average effect size estimate per egg (–0.05, Table 1) across a range of life histories, for a range of annual survival rates and clutch sizes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the meta-analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The effect size estimated in the meta-analysis (–0.05) resulted in a gain of fitness when reproductive output increased, especially in hypothetical species with low survival and small clutches.
source: Overall, the effect size estimated in the meta-analysis (–0.05) resulted in a gain of fitness when reproductive output increased, especially in hypothetical species with low survival and small clutches.
evidence: This is a finding from the fitness projection analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Using a stronger effect size (–0.15) led to a reduction in fitness in almost all cases.
source: If we used a stronger effect size (–0.15, the lower confidence interval of our meta-analysis), this led to a reduction in fitness in almost all cases.
evidence: This is a finding from the fitness projection analysis.

claim: The benefit of higher reproductive output was largely offset by the cost of survival when a species' survival rate and clutch size were high.
source: Conversely, the benefit of higher reproductive output was largely offset by the cost of survival when a species' survival rate and clutch size were high.
evidence: This is a finding from the fitness projection analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: When the effect size was increased up to fivefold, fitness costs of reproduction became more pronounced, but were still not present in species with small clutches and short lifespans.
source: When we increased the effect size up to fivefold, fitness costs of reproduction became more pronounced, but were still not present in species with small clutches and short lifespans.
evidence: This is a finding from the fitness projection analysis.

claim: Under long-term evolution, selection differentials should lead to individual hypothetical species moving towards the diagonal representing the fast–slow pace of life continuum.
source: Under long-term evolution, these selection differentials should lead to individual hypothetical species moving towards the diagonal (bottom-left to the right-top corner). This diagonal represents the observed fast–slow pace of life continuum observed among species (Healy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference from the fitness projections with citation to support the fast-slow continuum.

claim: In exemplar species, the selection differential was observed to lie slightly above one, indicating that individuals having a higher clutch size than the species' average would gain a slight fitness benefit.
source: In these exemplar species, the selection differential was observed to lie slightly above one, indicating that individuals having a higher clutch size than the species' average would gain a slight fitness benefit.
evidence: This is a finding from the fitness projection analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The fitness costs and benefits did not diverge substantially with the addition of chicks, but flattened.
source: The fitness costs and benefits did, in general, not diverge substantially with the addition of chicks, but flattened, suggesting that the costs of survival counterbalance the benefits of reproduction across a range of reproductive outputs within a species.
evidence: This is a finding from the fitness projection analysis.

claim: The low costs of reproduction estimated could still be responsible for between-species life-history evolution.
source: The low costs of reproduction that we estimated could still be responsible for between-species life-history evolution, constraining species reproductive output and survival combination to fall along the diagonal of the fast–slow pace of life continuum.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: Directional selection estimated in the wild often does not translate to inter-generational change on the population level.
source: Often directional selection estimated in the wild does not translate to the inter-generational change on the population level (Pujol et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Only far away from the diagonal did fitness projections reach a magnitude that would be predicted to lead to rapid evolutionary change.
source: Note, however, that only far away from the diagonal did our fitness projections reach a magnitude that would be predicted to lead to rapid evolutionary change (Gingerich, 2009; see Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the fitness projections with citation support.

claim: Within-species the minimal costs of reproduction, a flat fitness landscape and quality effects together explain why individuals appear to under-produce.
source: We argue that within-species the minimal costs of reproduction, a flat fitness landscape and quality effects (Figure 1) together explain why individuals appear to under-produce.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining multiple findings from the study.

claim: Only when individuals are pushed beyond the observed between-species constraint do costs become apparent.
source: Only when individuals are pushed beyond the observed between-species constraint do costs become apparent (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: A strong trade-off is observed between species, but within species this trade-off is not apparent.
source: A strong trade-off is observed between species, but within species this trade-off is not apparent and variation in reproductive output is maintained within fitness boundaries similar to those that determine the between-species life-history trade-off.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings from the meta-analysis and fitness projections.

claim: The costs of reproduction are likely to operate on a physiological level, but the fitness consequences will remain largely flat over a species' observed variation in reproductive output.
source: The implication of this conclusion is that the costs of reproduction are likely to operate on a physiological level, but that the fitness consequences will remain largely flat over a species' observed variation in reproductive output.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the results.

claim: The effects of quality are opposite in sign and magnitude to the cost of reproduction.
source: These effects are further obscured by the effects of quality (observational studies), which are opposite in sign and magnitude to the cost of reproduction (experimental studies) (Figure 1) and are likely to further flatten the fitness landscape.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Differences in individual quality drive variation in clutch size.
source: Our results provide the first meta-analytic evidence that differences in individual quality drive variation in clutch size and that parental survival costs do not constrain within-species variation in reproductive effort (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the meta-analysis.

claim: Parental survival costs do not constrain within-species variation in reproductive effort.
source: Our results provide the first meta-analytic evidence that differences in individual quality drive variation in clutch size and that parental survival costs do not constrain within-species variation in reproductive effort (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the meta-analysis.

claim: Quality is defined as a combination of traits that give an individual higher fitness.
source: Here, we use the definition of quality as a combination of traits that give an individual higher fitness (van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986).
evidence: This is a definition provided with citation support.

claim: Among-individual heterogeneity is a well-established effect across populations in ecology and evolution.
source: The finding of individual quality being a driver of variation in clutch size is not necessarily a surprising one, even though this contradicts the general theory that trade-offs drive variation in clutch size, as among-individual heterogeneity is also a well-established effect across populations in the field of ecology and evolution (such as age-specific reproductive performance) (van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986; Vedder and Bouwhuis, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Positive genetic correlations have been found in the wild and result from positive pleiotropy.
source: There has previously been discussion of why positive genetic correlations have been found in the wild and result from, for example, positive pleiotropy (Maklakov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Empirical data has found an absence of a trade-off between reproduction and survival.
source: Furthermore, empirical data has also found an absence of a trade-off between reproduction and survival (Reznick et al., 2004; Žák and Reichard, 2021; Kimber and Chippindale, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior empirical studies.

claim: A recent meta-analysis on genetic life-history trade-offs found several positive genetic correlations between survival and other life-history traits.
source: A recent meta-analysis on genetic life-history trade-offs found several positive genetic correlations between survival and other life-history traits, which is in conflict with life-history trade-off theory (Chang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent meta-analysis.

claim: Brood manipulations often fail to take into account that variation in resource acquisition may be larger than variation in resource allocation.
source: Brood manipulations often fail to take into account that variation in resource acquisition may be larger than variation in resource allocation, and though intuitively manipulation of effort tests variation in resource allocation, it fails to account for the baseline variation in reproductive performance (van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986).
evidence: This is a theoretical point supported by citation.

claim: Variation in resource allocation can be present and testable through experiments but may only account for a small proportion of variation observed in reproductive output.
source: This presents a fundamental flaw which our results demonstrate – variation in resource allocation can be present and testable through experiments (i.e. brood manipulations) but may only account for a small proportion of variation observed in reproductive output.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of theory.

claim: Jackdaws show costs of increased brood size only when applied sequentially across years.
source: Perhaps fitting with this interpretation or with additional costs from recurring bouts of enhanced reproductive effort, Jackdaws (Corvus monedula) show costs of increased brood size only when applied sequentially across years, but note that for this study there is no control group that is only manipulated in single years (Boonekamp et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Environmental variability likely leads to alternative phenotypes being selected for at different points in space and time.
source: The reason selection is not acting on 'high-quality' individuals is currently unknown, but it is likely that environmental variability leads to alternative phenotypes being selected for at different points in space and time (also discussed in Pujol et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation with citation support.

claim: The quality effect could represent a terminal effect, where individuals have lower reproductive output in the year preceding their death.
source: It is also possible that the quality effect could represent a terminal effect, where individuals have lower reproductive output in the year preceding their death, thereby driving the trend for naturally lower laying birds to have lower survival when estimated between individuals (e.g. Coulson and Fairweather, 2001; Rattiste, 2004; Simons et al., 2016; Coulson and Fairweather, 2001; Rattiste, 2004; Simons et al., 2016; also see Hammers et al., 2012 for age-related changes in reproductive output).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The effect on parental annual survival of having naturally larger clutches was significantly opposite to the result of increasing clutch size through brood manipulation and quantitatively similar.
source: The effect on parental annual survival of having naturally larger clutches was significantly opposite to the result of increasing clutch size through brood manipulation and quantitatively similar.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis.

claim: Parents with naturally larger clutches are expected to live longer, and this counterbalances the 'cost of reproduction' when their brood size is experimentally manipulated.
source: Parents with naturally larger clutches are thus expected to live longer, and this counterbalances the 'cost of reproduction' when their brood size is experimentally manipulated.
evidence: This is an inference from the meta-analysis results.

claim: It is possible that quality effects mask trade-offs.
source: It is, therefore, possible that quality effects mask trade-offs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: It could be possible that individuals that lay larger clutches have smaller costs of reproduction.
source: Furthermore, it could be possible that individuals that lay larger clutches have smaller costs of reproduction, that is, would respond less in terms of annual survival to a brood size manipulation, but with our current dataset we cannot address this hypothesis (Figure 5).
evidence: This is speculation about a hypothesis that cannot be tested with the current data.

claim: The effect of a change in clutch size on parental survival may be non-linear.
source: The effect of a change in clutch size on parental survival may also be non-linear, but it remains to be determined what shape, if not linear, the relationship would be.
evidence: This is speculation about potential non-linear relationships.

claim: Species that laid the smallest clutches showed the largest effects for both costs of reproduction and quality effects.
source: For both costs of reproduction and quality effects, we found that species that laid the smallest clutches showed the largest effects.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Brood manipulations that affect parental survival are likely to be the result of pushing parental effort beyond its natural optima.
source: Brood manipulations that affect parental survival are thus likely to be the result of pushing parental effort beyond its natural optima (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and so arguably that brood manipulations are not necessarily a good test of whether trade-offs happen in the wild.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The classic trade-off between adult survival and clutch size cared for is only apparent when an individual is forced to raise a clutch outside of its individual optimum.
source: The classic trade-off between adult survival and the clutch size cared for is only apparent when an individual is forced to raise a clutch outside of its individual optimum, and these effects are confounded or even fully counterbalanced by differences in quality (as theorised in van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with citation support.

claim: For current extant species, the within-species fitness landscape of the reproduction survival trade-off is flat.
source: Our fitness projections of the consequences of the costs of reproduction using the overall effect size we estimated suggest that, for current extant species, the within-species fitness landscape of the reproduction survival trade-off is flat.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the fitness projection analysis.

claim: Species' life-history decisions are constrained within a broader fast–slow life-history continuum.
source: Species' life-history decisions are constrained within a broader fast–slow life-history continuum, explaining why variation within species in reproductive effort, such as in clutch size, is large and near universal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of life-history theory.

claim: This analysis assumes that other fitness costs of reproduction are smaller or at least less relevant than survival costs.
source: Our interpretation also assumes that other fitness costs of reproduction are smaller or at least less relevant than survival costs.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption stated in the discussion.

claim: Effects on offspring quality, parental condition other than survival, and future reproductive effort have been observed.
source: However, it is possible that such costs are actually more important, and it should be noted that effects such as those on offspring quality (e.g. Conrad and Robertson, 1992 and Smith et al., 1989), parental condition other than survival (e.g. Reid, 1987 and Kalmbach et al., 2004), and future reproductive effort e.g. Järvistö et al., 2016 have been observed (also see Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The importance of effects on offspring quality, parental condition, and future reproductive effort is likely to vary considerably in different species.
source: However, the importance of these effects is likely to vary considerably in different species.
evidence: This is an inference about variation across species.

claim: The survival cost to reproduce is thought to be universal across both bird species and across taxa.
source: Conversely, the survival cost to reproduce is thought to be universal across both bird species and across taxa, and it is perhaps for this reason that the reproduction–survival trade-off has been considered to contribute more to variation in reproductive effort than other trade-offs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in life-history theory.

claim: Few studies that have measured the different domains that contribute to fitness in brood size manipulation studies concluded that only in combination do these costs result in balancing selection for the current most common brood size in the population.
source: Indeed, the few studies that have measured the different domains that contribute to fitness in brood size manipulation studies concluded that only in combination do these costs result in balancing selection for the current most common brood size in the population (Daan et al., 1990; Verhulst and Tinbergen, 1991; Tinbergen and Daan, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Classic trade-off explanations fail to explain why variation in reproductive effort is prevalent within species and why between-species life-history trade-offs appear so much stronger.
source: Such classic trade-off explanations do, however, fail to explain why variation in reproductive effort is prevalent within species and why between-species life-history trade-offs appear so much stronger and conclusive.
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of classic theory.

claim: At its optimum, the within-species trade-off between survival and reproduction is relatively flat, and thus neutral to selection.
source: Our analysis and interpretation suggest that, at its optimum, the within-species trade-off between survival and reproduction is relatively flat, and thus neutral to selection (supporting the theory presented in Cohen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with citation support.

claim: The lack of evidence supporting trade-offs driving within-species variation does not necessarily mean that physiological costs of reproduction are non-existent.
source: We suggest that the lack of evidence supporting trade-offs driving within-species variation does not necessarily mean that physiological costs of reproduction are non-existent (e.g. Smith et al., 1989 and Lemaître et al., 2015), but rather that, within the wild and within the natural range of reproductive activities, such costs are not relevant to fitness.
evidence: This is an interpretation with citation support.

claim: One key explanation for the flat fitness landscape is that individuals differ in quality.
source: One key explanation for this effect supported by our meta-analysis (Figure 5) and prior theory (van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986) is that individuals differ in quality.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by the meta-analysis results and prior theory.

claim: 78 individual effect sizes from 30 species and 46 papers were used in the meta-analysis.
source: From the literature search, 78 individual effect sizes from 30 species and 46 papers were used (20 observational and 58 experimental studies).
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the meta-analysis.

claim: The phylogeny was obtained using BEAST to measure a distribution of 1000 possible phylogenetic trees of the focal 30 species extracted from BirdTree.
source: The phylogeny was obtained using BEAST to measure a distribution of 1000 possible phylogenetic trees of the focal 30 species extracted from BirdTree (Rubolini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used with citation.

claim: Much of the data used in this analysis were taken from studies where these data were not the main focus of the study, which reduces the risk of publication bias.
source: Much of the data used in this analysis were taken from studies where these data were not the main focus of the study. This reduces the risk that our results are heavily influenced by a publication bias for positive results.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential for publication bias in the dataset.

claim: The relationship between clutch size and survival was significantly different between observational and brood manipulation studies with p<0.01.
source: The relationship between clutch size and survival was significantly different and opposite between observational and brood manipulation studies, irrespective of how clutch size was scaled (p<0.01, Figure 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the meta-analysis.

claim: For raw clutch size, the effect size for brood manipulation was –0.0522 with 95% CI [–0.1406, 0.0363] and p=0.2477.
source: Raw	Clutch size	Brood manipulation	–0.0522	–0.1406	0.0363	0.0007	(0.2477)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Table 1.

claim: For standardised clutch size, the effect size for brood manipulation was –0.0651 with 95% CI [–0.1478, 0.0177] and p=0.1232.
source: Standardised	Clutch size	Brood manipulation	–0.0651	–0.1478	0.0177	0.0065	(0.1232)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Table 1.

claim: For proportional clutch size, the effect size for brood manipulation was –0.2703 with 95% CI [–0.4984, –0.0423] and p=0.0202.
source: Proportional	Clutch size	Brood manipulation	–0.2703	–0.4984	–0.0423	0.0005	(0.0202)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Table 1.

claim: The interaction between treatment and species clutch size effect size was –0.036 with p=0.015.
source: Species with small clutch sizes showed stronger costs of reproduction and a stronger relationship with quality (Interaction between treatment and species clutch size effect size = –0.036, p=0.015).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the meta-analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The clutch size range across species included in the analysis was from 2 to 11.
source: Expressing clutch size as a proportional increase corrects for the variation in average clutch size observed across the species included in this analysis, which ranged from 2 to 11.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset.

claim: The parental effort required to raise two instead of one chick is potentially doubled.
source: The parental effort required to raise two instead of one chick is potentially doubled, whereas one additional chick in a brood of 11 is likely to require only a marginal increase in effort.
evidence: This is an inference about the proportional effort required for different clutch sizes.

claim: One additional chick in a brood of 11 is likely to require only a marginal increase in effort.
source: The parental effort required to raise two instead of one chick is potentially doubled, whereas one additional chick in a brood of 11 is likely to require only a marginal increase in effort.
evidence: This is an inference about the proportional effort required for different clutch sizes.
